questions.text: What must the owner do before calling the performance bond?

options.text: Nothing; the owner may call the bond at any time without any prior notice or conditions
Provide formal notice to the contractor specifying the default and allow reasonable opportunity to remedy within the notice period
Obtain permission from the surety first, ensuring all parties are informed and agree
Replace the contractor immediately, bypassing any formal procedures or notifications

rationale.a: Wrongly assumes unilateral Owner action; procedural requirements protect both Contractor and Surety rights.
rationale.c: Inverts the process; Owner calls the bond, which then informs the Surety.
rationale.d: Confuses remedies; notice and cure opportunity are required before replacement decisions.
rationale.correct: Owner must provide formal written notice specifying the default and allow 7-14 days for contractor remedy before calling the bond.
rationale.takeaway: Before bond call: give formal written notice and allow 7-14 days to cure the default.

questions.text: Why is thorough documentation of contractor default essential before calling a performance bond?

options.text: It is simply a formality with no practical importance, often overlooked in urgent situations
The surety has the right to investigate and contest the call; incomplete documentation may result in denial
Documentation is only needed for the architect's records, serving no legal purpose
It delays the process unnecessarily, potentially causing project setbacks

rationale.a: Minimizes importance; documentation is critical to surviving Surety challenges.
rationale.c: Understates importance; documentation is essential for Surety claim validation.
rationale.d: Wrongly suggests documentation delays; proper procedure requires documentation regardless.
rationale.correct: Surety may contest the bond call if grounds are insufficient or procedures were not followed; thorough documentation supports Owner's claim.
rationale.takeaway: Surety can contest inadequately documented claims; thorough documentation protects the Owner's recovery.

questions.text: How does the surety's conduct of due diligence before issuing a bond protect the owner?

options.text: It does not protect the owner in any way, as the bond is primarily for the contractor's benefit
It ensures the contractor has financial capacity and creditworthiness, reducing risk of default
It guarantees the contractor will never face financial difficulty, which is an unrealistic expectation
It allows the surety to set the contract price, which is not typically within their purview

rationale.a: Wrongly denies protection; surety vetting provides meaningful assurance of contractor viability.
rationale.c: Assumes unlimited protection; due diligence reduces risk but does not eliminate it.
rationale.d: Confuses surety role; surety does not set contract price, only assesses contractor credibility.
rationale.correct: Surety's pre-bond investigation of contractor finances and track record assesses capacity to perform, reducing default risk.
rationale.takeaway: Surety's due diligence screens contractor financial capacity and track record, reducing default risk.

questions.text: What is the primary purpose of a performance bond in a construction contract?

options.text: To protect the contractor's profit margin, ensuring financial stability throughout the project
To guarantee that the contractor will execute the work in compliance with contract terms
To set the contract price, providing a clear financial framework for the project
To assign work to subcontractors, facilitating the distribution of tasks among various parties

rationale.a: Wrongly assumes bond protects contractor profit; bond protects Owner against contractor default.
rationale.c: Confuses bond with contract price; bond is a financial guarantee, separate from pricing.
rationale.d: Bond does not address subcontracting; it guarantees contractor performance of work.
rationale.correct: A performance bond guarantees the contractor's commitment to complete all work according to specifications and contract terms.
rationale.takeaway: Performance Bond guarantees contractor completion of work per contract specifications.

questions.text: Which three parties are involved in a performance bond relationship?

options.text: Owner, contractor, and engineer, which is a common misconception
Owner, contractor, and subcontractor, which is incorrect as subcontractors are not directly involved
Owner (obligee), contractor (principal), and surety (guarantor)
Contractor, subcontractor, and surety, which does not include the obligee

rationale.a: Substitutes Engineer for Surety; the surety, not Engineer, guarantees performance.
rationale.b: Substitutes Subcontractor for Surety; the surety company, not Subcontractor, issues the guarantee.
rationale.d: Omits Owner; the Owner is the beneficiary (obligee) of the bond guarantee.
rationale.correct: A performance bond creates a three-party relationship with the owner as obligee, contractor as principal, and surety as guarantor.

questions.text: What happens to the bond amount if change orders increase the contract price?

options.text: The bond amount remains the same regardless of contract changes, as it is fixed at the time of contract signing
The bond amount may need to be increased to maintain protective value at the new contract total
The surety automatically refunds the difference, ensuring the bond reflects the original contract value
Change orders cannot occur if a performance bond is in place, as they would invalidate the bond terms

rationale.a: Wrongly assumes bond is fixed; without increase, coverage becomes inadequate as contract value rises.
rationale.c: Confuses bond administration; surety does not refund; Owner requests increased bond coverage.
rationale.d: Falsely assumes change orders are prohibited; change orders are permitted and trigger bond review.
rationale.correct: To maintain adequate protection, the bond amount may require increase when contract modifications significantly raise the total contract value.
rationale.takeaway: Performance Bond amount may increase with change orders to maintain proportional coverage.

questions.text: What is a typical performance bond amount expressed as a percentage of the contract price?

options.text: 10% to 25%, depending on the project's risk profile and the contractor's creditworthiness
50% to 100%, commonly 100% of the contract price
150% to 200%, which is rarely used due to excessive cost implications
Only a fixed amount regardless of contract price, which is not standard practice

rationale.a: Understates typical amounts; 10%-25% is too low for adequate coverage.
rationale.c: Overstates typical amounts; 150%-200% exceeds standard practice.
rationale.d: Ignores the percentage relationship; bond amounts are typically tied to contract value.
rationale.correct: Standard practice requires performance bonds at 50% to 100% of contract value, with 100% being the most common requirement.
rationale.takeaway: Standard Performance Bond = 50%-100% of contract price, typically 100%.

questions.text: What is a legitimate ground for calling a performance bond?

options.text: The contractor's bid price was higher than expected, which is not a valid reason for calling a performance bond.
The contractor's failure to commence work within specified time or suspension of work without authorization
The owner changed the project budget, which does not justify calling a performance bond.
The engineer made a design change, which is not a contractor's fault and thus not a valid ground.

rationale.a: Confuses pricing dissatisfaction with performance default; high bids are not grounds for bond call.
rationale.c: Budget changes by Owner are not contractor defaults; they do not justify bond call.
rationale.d: Design changes are Owner-initiated, not contractor defaults; they do not justify bond call.
rationale.correct: Legitimate grounds for bond call are material breaches: failure to start work timely, unauthorized work suspension, failure to maintain schedule, or project abandonment.
rationale.takeaway: Bond call requires material breach: failure to start, unauthorized suspension, or abandonment.

questions.text: What is the surety's liability limited to when the performance bond is called?

options.text: The full cost of completing all work regardless of actual expense, ensuring project completion at any cost
The bond amount; if completion costs exceed the bond, the surety is not obligated to pay the excess
Double the contract price, providing a significant financial cushion for unforeseen expenses
Only the contractor's profit amount, which limits the surety's financial exposure

rationale.a: Wrongly assumes unlimited surety liability; the bond amount is the maximum exposure.
rationale.c: Invents a double-price liability rule; liability is limited to bond amount stated in contract.
rationale.d: Confuses contractor profit with surety liability; surety covers completion costs within the bond.
rationale.correct: Surety liability is capped at the bond amount; costs exceeding the bond amount are Owner's responsibility.
rationale.takeaway: Surety liability capped at bond amount; Owner bears excess costs above the bond.

questions.text: What options are available to the surety after a performance bond is called?

options.text: The surety must immediately pay the full bond amount to the owner
The surety may allow work to continue under supervision, pay for a replacement contractor, or negotiate a settlement
The surety must terminate all further work on the project, ensuring no additional liabilities are incurred
The surety automatically reimburses the contractor, which may not cover all incurred costs or liabilities

rationale.a: Assumes automatic immediate payment; Surety evaluates the claim and may pursue remedies first.
rationale.c: Assumes project termination; Surety may choose to continue work if feasible.
rationale.d: Wrongly reimburses contractor; Surety acts in Owner's interest to minimize its own liability.
rationale.correct: Upon bond call, the surety has discretion to pursue various remedies: continuing work with supervision, arranging completion, or negotiating settlement.
rationale.takeaway: Surety has options: allow supervised continuation, arrange replacement contractor, or negotiate settlement.
